subject: physics

items.q: Kepler's third law describes the orbits of the planets around the Sun. Taking each orbit as a circle of radius r with time period T, which statement expresses the law?
items.correct: T²/r³ has the same value for every planet that orbits the Sun.
items.misconception: T/r has the same value for every planet that orbits the Sun.
items.why: Everyday experience of travel is that a longer journey at a steady speed takes proportionally longer, and diagrams of the Solar System give no sense of the planets' different speeds. Proportional reasoning (double the distance, double the time) is the default students reach for. Kepler's third law, T² ∝ r³, gives T ∝ r^(3/2). With v = 2πr/T this means v ∝ r/r^(3/2) = 1/√r: the further out, the slower. Outer planets therefore take longer both because their path is longer and because they move more slowly. Neptune is about 30 times further from the Sun than the Earth and moves at about one fifth of the Earth's speed.
items.specStatementText: Kepler’s three laws of orbital motion
items.random_wrong: T has the same value for every planet, whatever its distance.

items.q: A comet moves around the Sun in a highly elliptical orbit. Which statement about the comet agrees with Kepler's laws?
items.correct: It moves fastest when it is nearest the Sun.
items.misconception: It moves at the same speed at every point of its orbit.
items.why: Students first meet orbits as circles, in which the speed is constant, and 'equal … in equal times' sounds like the description of a steady speed. The word 'areas' is read past. A thin triangle swept out near the Sun is short, so to have the same area as one swept far from the Sun its arc must be longer. The planet therefore covers a longer arc in the same time when near the Sun: it moves fastest at its closest approach and slowest at its furthest point.
items.specStatementText: Kepler’s three laws of orbital motion
items.random_wrong: It moves fastest when it is furthest from the Sun.

items.q: Io and Europa are moons of Jupiter, and their orbits may be taken as circular. Io has an orbital radius of 4.22 × 10⁸ m and a time period of 1.77 days. Europa has an orbital radius of 6.71 × 10⁸ m. What is the time period of Europa?
items.correct: 3.55 days
items.misconception: 1.77 days
items.why:
Rigid rotation (wheels, turntables, merry-go-rounds) is the rotation students know best, and in circular-motion lessons v = ωr is used with the same ω for every point. Pictures of the Solar System as a neat set of rings encourage the image of a turning disc. Orbiting bodies are not joined together, so nothing forces them to share an angular speed. Gravity alone sets each one's motion: in a circular orbit ω = √(GM/r³), which falls with distance. The Moon takes 27 days to orbit the Earth, while a satellite in low orbit takes about 90 minutes; the outer planets take decades to orbit the Sun.

Working: Kepler's third law for two moons of the same planet: T_E²/r_E³ = T_I²/r_I³ ⇒ T_E = T_I (r_E/r_I)^(3/2). r_E/r_I = 6.71 × 10⁸ m / 4.22 × 10⁸ m = 1.590; 1.590^(3/2) = 2.005. T_E = 1.77 days × 2.005 = 3.55 days.
items.specStatementText: Kepler’s three laws of orbital motion
items.random_wrong: 2.81 days
items.working: Kepler's third law for two moons of the same planet: T_E²/r_E³ = T_I²/r_I³ ⇒ T_E = T_I (r_E/r_I)^(3/2). r_E/r_I = 6.71 × 10⁸ m / 4.22 × 10⁸ m = 1.590; 1.590^(3/2) = 2.005. T_E = 1.77 days × 2.005 = 3.55 days.

items.q: The Earth exerts a gravitational force of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on the Moon. The mass of the Moon is about 1.2% of the mass of the Earth. Which statement about the gravitational force that the Moon exerts on the Earth is correct?
items.correct: It is 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, and it pulls the Earth towards the Moon.
items.misconception: It is about 1.2% of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, as the Moon has far less mass.
items.why:
The effects are very unequal: the Moon orbits the Earth, while the Earth hardly moves. Students infer unequal forces from unequal effects, and everyday language says the Earth 'holds' the Moon, as if the pull were one-way. This is one of the most widely reported Newton's third law misconceptions. The forces are equal; their effects differ because a = F/m. The same force gives the Moon about 81 times the acceleration it gives the Earth. The Earth does move in response: both bodies orbit their common centre of mass, which lies about 4700 km from the Earth's centre.

Working: Newton's third law: F(Moon on Earth) = F(Earth on Moon) = 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, opposite in direction. F = Gm₁m₂/r² is symmetric in m₁ and m₂, so the mass ratio (1.2%) does not enter.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s universal law of gravitation as given by F = G m₁m₂/r² for bodies treated as point masses
items.random_wrong: It is zero, as a small body cannot attract a much larger one.
items.working: Newton's third law: F(Moon on Earth) = F(Earth on Moon) = 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, opposite in direction. F = Gm₁m₂/r² is symmetric in m₁ and m₂, so the mass ratio (1.2%) does not enter.

items.q: A satellite of mass 1200 kg orbits the Earth at a height of 600 km above the surface. The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6370 km. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the gravitational force that the Earth exerts on the satellite?
items.why:
Heights in everyday life, and in ΔE_p = mgΔh, are measured from the ground, and orbits are usually described by their altitude ('400 km up'). The model of a sphere as a point mass at its centre is not connected with where r is measured from. A uniform sphere acts as a point mass at its centre, so every distance in these equations is measured from the centre: r = R + h. A satellite 400 km above the Earth is at r = 6370 km + 400 km = 6770 km, not 400 km.

Working: r = R + h = 6370 km + 600 km = 6970 km = 6.97 × 10⁶ m. F = GMm/r² = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)(5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)(1200 kg)/(6.97 × 10⁶ m)² = 4.778 × 10¹⁷ / 4.858 × 10¹³ = 9.84 × 10³ N.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s universal law of gravitation as given by F = G m₁m₂/r² for bodies treated as point masses

items.q: A planet is a sphere of uniform density. Why can it be treated as a point mass at its centre when calculating the gravitational force on a satellite orbiting it?
items.correct: At any point outside a uniform sphere, its field is that of a point mass at its centre.
items.misconception: A satellite is usually far away compared with the planet's radius, so the planet looks like a point.
items.why: Students meet the point-mass idea as 'things far away look like points', which is true for bodies of any shape, and are not told that a uniform sphere is a special case in which the result is exact at every external point. Two separate conditions allow an extended body to be treated as a point mass: (1) it is a uniform sphere (or spherically symmetric) and the point is outside it, at any distance; or (2) the separation is very large compared with its size. Satellites in low orbit are only about 1.06 Earth radii from the Earth's centre, yet the point-mass model is exact for them by condition (1).
items.specStatementText: conditions under which extended bodies can be treated as point masses
items.random_wrong: The satellite's mass is tiny compared with the planet's, so the planet's size is irrelevant.

items.q: Which statement defines the gravitational field strength g at a point?
items.correct: The gravitational force per unit mass on a small point mass placed at that point.
items.misconception: The gravitational force acting on any object placed at that point, in newtons.
items.why:
In everyday speech 'strong gravity' means a strong pull, and students meet g first inside W = mg without separating the field from the force. A heavier object does feel a larger force, which is mistaken for a stronger field. The field is a property of the point in space, set by the mass producing it: g = GM/r². The force on an object at that point is mg. Doubling the object's mass doubles the force but leaves g, the force per kilogram, unchanged.

Working: Definition: g = F/m, the force per unit mass on a small test mass; unit N kg⁻¹ (= m s⁻²). The value 9.8 m s⁻² applies only at the Earth's surface.
items.specStatementText: that gravitational field strength g at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by g = F/m = GM/r²
items.random_wrong: The acceleration of free fall at that point, which is 9.8 m s⁻² at every point.
items.working: Definition: g = F/m, the force per unit mass on a small test mass; unit N kg⁻¹ (= m s⁻²). The value 9.8 m s⁻² applies only at the Earth's surface.

items.q: At the surface of the Earth, g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹. Planet X has the same mass as the Earth but half its radius. Both may be treated as uniform spheres. What is the gravitational field strength at the surface of planet X?
items.correct: 39.2 N kg⁻¹
items.misconception: 19.6 N kg⁻¹
items.why:
Inverse proportion is the simplest 'more distance, less pull' relationship, and students often forget to square r when scaling. The square is also dropped when r² is split across a ratio. Write the ratio out in full: g₂/g₁ = (M₂/M₁)(r₁/r₂)². The inverse-square law follows from the field spreading out over the area of a sphere, 4πr², which grows as the square of the radius.

Working: g = GM/R². g_X/g_E = (M_X/M_E)(R_E/R_X)² = 1 × 2² = 4. g_X = 4 × 9.8 N kg⁻¹ = 39.2 N kg⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that gravitational field strength g at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by g = F/m = GM/r²
items.random_wrong: 9.80 N kg⁻¹
items.working: g = GM/R². g_X/g_E = (M_X/M_E)(R_E/R_X)² = 1 × 2² = 4. g_X = 4 × 9.8 N kg⁻¹ = 39.2 N kg⁻¹.

items.q: The Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) and the Moon (mass 7.35 × 10²² kg) are 3.84 × 10⁸ m apart, centre to centre. At one point on the line joining their centres, the resultant gravitational field strength is zero. How far is this point from the centre of the Earth?
items.why:
Symmetric examples (two equal masses or two equal charges) are the ones usually drawn, and 'balance' is associated with the middle. Set the two field magnitudes equal: GM₁/x² = GM₂/(d − x)², so x/(d − x) = √(M₁/M₂). For the Earth and the Moon (mass ratio 81) the point is nine times further from the Earth than from the Moon, about 90% of the way to the Moon.

Working: Fields are antiparallel on the line joining the centres, so the resultant is zero where GM_E/x² = GM_M/(d − x)². √(M_E/M_M) = √(5.97 × 10²⁴ / 7.35 × 10²²) = √81.2 = 9.01. x = 9.01(d − x) ⇒ x = 9.01 × 3.84 × 10⁸ m / 10.01 = 3.46 × 10⁸ m from the Earth's centre.
items.specStatementText: that gravitational field strength g at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by g = F/m = GM/r²
items.working: Fields are antiparallel on the line joining the centres, so the resultant is zero where GM_E/x² = GM_M/(d − x)². √(M_E/M_M) = √(5.97 × 10²⁴ / 7.35 × 10²²) = √81.2 = 9.01. x = 9.01(d − x) ⇒ x = 9.01 × 3.84 × 10⁸ m / 10.01 = 3.46 × 10⁸ m from the Earth's centre.

items.q: A student sketches the gravitational field lines around an isolated planet that is a uniform sphere. Which description of a correct sketch is right?
items.correct: Straight radial lines pointing inwards to the planet's centre, closer together near its surface.
items.misconception: Straight radial lines pointing outwards from the planet's centre, closer together near it.
items.why: Electric field patterns around positive charges, and magnetic lines leaving a north pole, are drawn pointing outwards, and students transfer the pattern. A 'source' of a field is thought of as sending something out. The direction of a field line is the direction of the force on a small test mass. Gravity attracts, so the arrows on a planet's field lines point inwards to its centre. Gravitational fields have no equivalent of a positive charge; they only ever point towards masses.
items.specStatementText: gravitational field lines.
items.random_wrong: Parallel lines all pointing 'down' in one direction, equally spaced at all distances.

items.q: Close to the surface of a planet, over a region a few kilometres across, the gravitational field is drawn as parallel, equally spaced field lines pointing vertically downwards. What does this pattern show about the field in that region?
items.correct: The field strength has the same size and direction at every point in the region.
items.misconception: Any object released or thrown in the region moves along one of the field lines.
items.why: Field lines look like tracks, and in many diagrams a dropped object does fall along one. Students also confuse the direction of force with the direction of velocity, the same confusion behind 'motion implies force'. Field lines give the direction of the force, and hence of the acceleration. The velocity can be in any direction: a ball thrown horizontally has a velocity across the lines and follows a parabola, while a satellite moves at right angles to the radial field lines.
items.specStatementText: gravitational field lines.
items.random_wrong: The field acts only along the lines drawn, with no field in the gaps between them.

items.q: The gravitational potential energy E_p of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of its components. Why is E_p of an Earth–satellite system negative?
items.correct: The bodies attract, so the work done to bring them together from infinity is negative.
items.misconception: The minus sign shows that the potential energy is directed towards the centre of the Earth.
items.why: Students meet minus signs mostly as directions for vectors (velocity, displacement, force) and carry this reading to every minus sign in physics. Energy and potential are scalars. The minus sign is a statement about value: to separate the bodies to infinity, where E_p = 0, positive work must be done, so the E_p of any bound system is less than zero.
items.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential energy E_p of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of the components of the system
items.random_wrong: Positive work is needed to bring them together, so the minus sign is only a convention.

items.q: A satellite of mass 500 kg is moved from a circular orbit of radius 6.80 × 10⁶ m to a circular orbit of radius 2.04 × 10⁷ m around the Earth, of mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². The gravitational field strength at the Earth's surface is 9.8 N kg⁻¹. What is the change in the gravitational potential energy of the Earth–satellite system?
items.why:
Students compare magnitudes and ignore the sign. Near the surface they know E_p increases with height, but with negative values 'smaller number' is misread as 'less energy'. Compare signed values: −2.9 × 10¹⁰ J is less than −1.0 × 10¹⁰ J. ΔE_p = E_p,final − E_p,initial = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂), which is positive when r₂ > r₁. Work must be done against gravity to move a mass outwards, so its potential energy rises.

Working: GMm = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)(500 kg) = 1.991 × 10¹⁷ J m. E_p,initial = −1.991 × 10¹⁷/6.80 × 10⁶ = −2.928 × 10¹⁰ J; E_p,final = −1.991 × 10¹⁷/2.04 × 10⁷ = −9.76 × 10⁹ J. ΔE_p = −9.76 × 10⁹ − (−2.928 × 10¹⁰) = +1.95 × 10¹⁰ J.
items.specStatementText: the gravitational potential energy for a two-body system as given by E_p = −G m₁m₂/r where r is the separation between the centre of mass of the two bodies

items.q: A probe of mass m is lifted from the surface of a planet of radius R to a height R above the surface. The field strength at the surface is g. A student calculates the gain in gravitational potential energy using ΔE_p = mgΔh with Δh = R. How does the student's answer compare with the true gain, found from E_p = −GMm/r?
items.correct: 2.0 times the true gain
items.misconception: 1.0 times the true gain
items.why:
ΔE_p = mgΔh is used in every mechanics problem before gravitational fields are met, and it is not always stressed that it depends on a uniform field. g falls as 1/r², so over large distances the force, and the work done per metre, becomes smaller with height. mgΔh with the surface g therefore overestimates the change. Use ΔE_p = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂); it reduces to mgΔh only when Δh is much smaller than the radius.

Working: True ΔE_p = GMm(1/R − 1/2R) = GMm/2R. With GM = gR²: ΔE_p = mgR/2. Student: mgΔh = mgR. Ratio = mgR ÷ (mgR/2) = 2.0.
items.specStatementText: the gravitational potential energy for a two-body system as given by E_p = −G m₁m₂/r where r is the separation between the centre of mass of the two bodies
items.random_wrong: 4.0 times the true gain
items.working: True ΔE_p = GMm(1/R − 1/2R) = GMm/2R. With GM = gR²: ΔE_p = mgR/2. Student: mgΔh = mgR. Ratio = mgR ÷ (mgR/2) = 2.0.

items.q: Which statement about the gravitational potential V_g at a point outside a planet is correct?
items.correct: It is the work done per unit mass to bring a small mass from infinity to the point, and is negative.
items.misconception: It is the gravitational potential energy of any mass at the point, measured in joules.
items.why: The names are almost identical and both are introduced with work done from infinity. Students drop the 'per unit mass' in the definition of V_g. Check units: V_g in J kg⁻¹, E_p in J. The potential is set by the field (V_g = −GM/r); the potential energy also depends on the mass placed there (E_p = mV_g). To find work or energy, always multiply the potential or potential difference by the mass.
items.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential V_g at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point as given by V_g = −GM/r
items.random_wrong: It is zero at the planet's surface and increases with height above it, as mgh does.

items.q: The Moon has mass 7.35 × 10²² kg and radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the gravitational potential due to the Moon at a point 1.00 × 10⁶ m above its surface?
items.why:
g = GM/R² is often first met as the equation for the surface field, with R the planet's radius, and students carry R into every calculation. Values such as g = 9.8 N kg⁻¹ are used so often that they seem to hold at any height. Use r = R + h for a point at height h. At the height of a geostationary satellite (r ≈ 6.6 R) the field is only about 1/44 of its surface value. Only for points on the surface does r equal R.

Working: r = R + h = 1.74 × 10⁶ m + 1.00 × 10⁶ m = 2.74 × 10⁶ m. V_g = −GM/r = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)(7.35 × 10²² kg)/(2.74 × 10⁶ m) = −4.902 × 10¹² / 2.74 × 10⁶ = −1.79 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential V_g at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point as given by V_g = −GM/r

items.q: Two equipotential surfaces around the Earth are 1.00 × 10⁵ m apart along a radial line. The inner surface has V_g = −6.251 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹ and the outer surface has V_g = −6.155 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. Taking r as increasing outwards from the Earth's centre, what is the average gravitational field strength g between the two surfaces?
items.correct: −9.6 N kg⁻¹ (directed towards the Earth)
items.misconception: +9.6 N kg⁻¹ (directed away from the Earth)
items.why:
The minus sign is easily dropped when the gradient is calculated, and students picture things 'going up the potential' as the natural direction. Masses fall to lower potential energy, just as they fall downwards near the Earth. The minus sign in g = −ΔV_g/Δr expresses this: if V_g increases outwards (ΔV_g/Δr positive), g is negative, pointing inwards towards the mass.

Working: ΔV_g = V_outer − V_inner = −6.155 × 10⁷ − (−6.251 × 10⁷) = +9.6 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Δr = +1.00 × 10⁵ m. g = −ΔV_g/Δr = −9.6 N kg⁻¹, i.e. 9.6 N kg⁻¹ directed towards the Earth.
items.specStatementText: the gravitational field strength g as the gravitational potential gradient as given by g = −ΔV_g/Δr
items.random_wrong: −9.8 N kg⁻¹ (directed towards the Earth’s centre)
items.working: ΔV_g = V_outer − V_inner = −6.155 × 10⁷ − (−6.251 × 10⁷) = +9.6 × 10⁵ J kg⁻¹. Δr = +1.00 × 10⁵ m. g = −ΔV_g/Δr = −9.6 N kg⁻¹, i.e. 9.6 N kg⁻¹ directed towards the Earth.

items.q: An external force moves a 3.0 kg mass at constant speed from a point where the gravitational potential is −3.2 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ to a point where it is −1.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. What is the work done on the mass by the external force?
items.why:
The value of V_g at a point is what is usually calculated first, and students confuse 'potential' with 'potential difference', a confusion also widely reported in electricity. Only changes in potential are physically meaningful: g = −ΔV_g/Δr and W = mΔV_g. The value at one point includes the whole journey from infinity, which is not the journey being considered. Always subtract the two values.

Working: ΔV_g = V_final − V_initial = −1.1 × 10⁶ − (−3.2 × 10⁶) = +2.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. W = mΔV_g = 3.0 kg × 2.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ = +6.3 × 10⁶ J.
items.specStatementText: the work done in moving a mass m in a gravitational field as given by W = mΔV_g
items.working: ΔV_g = V_final − V_initial = −1.1 × 10⁶ − (−3.2 × 10⁶) = +2.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. W = mΔV_g = 3.0 kg × 2.1 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ = +6.3 × 10⁶ J.

items.q: An 800 kg satellite is launched from rest on the surface of a non-rotating planet of mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m, and placed in a circular orbit of radius 1.00 × 10⁷ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Ignoring air resistance, what is the minimum energy that must be supplied to the satellite?
items.why:
Satellites are thought of as 'up there' above the atmosphere, where many students believe there is no gravity to pull them down. The sideways speed of an orbit is not part of the everyday picture. An orbit is continuous free fall with a sideways speed large enough that the satellite keeps missing the planet. At orbital radius r, the satellite needs E_k = GMm/2r in addition to the gain in E_p. For orbits a few thousand km up, these two are of similar size.

Working: GMm = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(5.97 × 10²⁴)(800) = 3.186 × 10¹⁷ J m. Initial energy (rest, non-rotating planet): E = −GMm/R = −5.001 × 10¹⁰ J. Final energy in circular orbit: E = −GMm/2r = −1.593 × 10¹⁰ J. Energy supplied = −1.593 × 10¹⁰ − (−5.001 × 10¹⁰) = 3.41 × 10¹⁰ J (ΔE_p = 1.82 × 10¹⁰ J plus E_k = 1.59 × 10¹⁰ J).
items.specStatementText: the work done in moving a mass m in a gravitational field as given by W = mΔV_g
items.working: GMm = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹)(5.97 × 10²⁴)(800) = 3.186 × 10¹⁷ J m. Initial energy (rest, non-rotating planet): E = −GMm/R = −5.001 × 10¹⁰ J. Final energy in circular orbit: E = −GMm/2r = −1.593 × 10¹⁰ J. Energy supplied = −1.593 × 10¹⁰ − (−5.001 × 10¹⁰) = 3.41 × 10¹⁰ J (ΔE_p = 1.82 × 10¹⁰ J plus E_k = 1.59 × 10¹⁰ J).

items.q: Equipotential surfaces are drawn around an isolated planet that is a uniform sphere, at equal intervals of gravitational potential. Which description is correct?
items.correct: Concentric spheres, further apart the further they are from the planet.
items.misconception: Concentric spheres, equally spaced at all distances from the planet's centre.
items.why: The first equipotentials students draw are in a uniform field (near the surface, or between parallel plates in electricity), where equal steps are equally spaced. The pattern is transferred to the radial field. V_g = −GM/r, so r = GM/|V_g|. For equally spaced values of V_g, r increases by larger and larger amounts. Equipotential spacing mirrors the field strength: closely spaced where g is strong, widely spaced where g is weak.
items.specStatementText: equipotential surfaces for gravitational fields
items.random_wrong: Radial straight lines that point inwards towards the planet's centre.

items.q: A small mass is moved along an equipotential surface in a gravitational field. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The field is perpendicular to its path, so gravity does no work on the mass.
items.misconception: There is no gravitational field on the surface, so no force acts on the mass.
items.why: Students correctly learn that no work is done moving along an equipotential, and wrongly conclude that there is no force. The potential gradient is zero along the surface, which is misread as zero in every direction. The potential changes as you move across equipotentials, not along them. The field (−potential gradient) is therefore perpendicular to the surface; its magnitude is the change in V_g between neighbouring surfaces divided by their separation. A satellite in a circular orbit moves along an equipotential under a large gravitational force.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between equipotential surfaces and gravitational field lines
items.random_wrong: Gravity does work on the mass, as its weight acts on it all the time it moves.

items.q: The Moon has mass 7.35 × 10²² kg and radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the escape speed from a point 2.00 × 10⁶ m above the Moon's surface?
items.why:
Escape speed is usually quoted as a single number for each planet ('the escape speed of the Earth is 11.2 km s⁻¹'), so students treat it as a property of the planet rather than of a point in its field. Escape speed is set by the energy needed to reach infinity from where the body is: ½mv² = GMm/r. Further out, less energy is needed, so v_esc = √(2GM/r) is smaller. Use r = R + h for a point above the surface.

Working: r = R + h = 1.74 × 10⁶ m + 2.00 × 10⁶ m = 3.74 × 10⁶ m. GM = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 7.35 × 10²² = 4.902 × 10¹² N m² kg⁻¹. v_esc = √(2GM/r) = √(9.805 × 10¹² / 3.74 × 10⁶) = √(2.621 × 10⁶ m² s⁻²) = 1.62 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the escape speed v_esc at any point in a gravitational field as given by v_esc = √(2GM/r)

items.q: A satellite is in a circular orbit around a planet and has kinetic energy E_k. What is the minimum extra energy that must be given to the satellite for it to escape the gravitational influence of the planet?
items.correct: E_k, which raises its total energy from −E_k to zero
items.misconception: 2E_k, the magnitude of its gravitational potential energy
items.why:
From the surface, escape does need energy equal to |E_p| (starting from rest), and students carry this over to an orbiting satellite, forgetting the kinetic energy it already has. Escape condition: E_k + E_p ≥ 0. In orbit E_k = GMm/2r and E_p = −GMm/r, so the total is −GMm/2r. Raising it to zero needs +GMm/2r, which equals the satellite's current E_k: doubling its kinetic energy is enough.

Working: Circular orbit: E_k = GMm/2r, E_p = −GMm/r = −2E_k, E_total = −E_k. Escape requires E_total ≥ 0, so the minimum extra energy is E_k (v rises from v_orbital to √2 v_orbital = v_esc).
items.specStatementText: the escape speed v_esc at any point in a gravitational field as given by v_esc = √(2GM/r)
items.random_wrong: 3E_k, since escape speed is twice the orbital speed
items.working: Circular orbit: E_k = GMm/2r, E_p = −GMm/r = −2E_k, E_total = −E_k. Escape requires E_total ≥ 0, so the minimum extra energy is E_k (v rises from v_orbital to √2 v_orbital = v_esc).

items.q: A navigation satellite orbits the Earth in a circular orbit at a height of 2.02 × 10⁷ m above the surface. The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². What is the orbital speed of the satellite?
items.why:
Satellites are said to be 'in space', astronauts appear weightless, and launches are described as 'escaping Earth's gravity'. This fits the widely reported belief that there is no gravity in space. Without gravity a satellite would move off in a straight line. Gravity supplies exactly the centripetal force needed: GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v_orbital = √(GM/r). Escape needs √2 times this speed, v_esc = √(2GM/r), which would take the satellite to infinity and out of orbit.

Working: r = R + h = 6.37 × 10⁶ m + 2.02 × 10⁷ m = 2.657 × 10⁷ m. GM = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ = 3.982 × 10¹⁴ N m² kg⁻¹. v_orbital = √(GM/r) = √(1.499 × 10⁷ m² s⁻²) = 3.87 × 10³ m s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the orbital speed v_orbital of a body orbiting a large mass as given by v_orbital = √(GM/r)

items.q: A satellite is moved from one circular orbit to another circular orbit of larger radius around the same planet. How does its total energy in the new orbit compare with its total energy in the old orbit?
items.correct: Greater, because its potential energy rises by twice as much as its kinetic energy falls.
items.misconception: Greater, because it moves faster in the larger orbit and so has more kinetic energy.
items.why: More energy is associated with more speed, and the rocket firing needed to raise an orbit seems to speed the satellite up. Students do not separate kinetic and potential energy in orbit. In a circular orbit E_k = GMm/2r, which falls as r increases, while E_p = −GMm/r rises by twice as much. The total, −GMm/2r, rises. So raising an orbit needs energy but leaves the satellite slower: the Moon orbits at about 1 km s⁻¹, a low-orbit satellite at about 7.7 km s⁻¹.
items.specStatementText: the orbital speed v_orbital of a body orbiting a large mass as given by v_orbital = √(GM/r)
items.random_wrong: Lower, because it moves more slowly in the larger orbit and so has less kinetic energy.

items.q: A satellite in a low circular orbit experiences a small viscous drag force from the thin upper atmosphere. Over many orbits its path remains approximately circular. How do its orbital radius and its speed change?
items.correct: The radius gradually decreases while the orbital speed gradually increases.
items.misconception: The radius gradually decreases and the orbital speed also decreases.
items.why: In everyday experience friction and air resistance always slow things down, and 'the satellite loses energy' is read as 'the satellite loses speed'. As the satellite spirals slowly inwards, gravity does positive work on it that exceeds the negative work done by drag. Its total energy −GMm/2r falls (more negative), its radius falls, and its speed √(GM/r) rises. This is known as the satellite drag paradox.
items.specStatementText: the qualitative effect of a small viscous drag force due to the atmosphere on the height and speed of an orbiting body.
items.random_wrong: The radius gradually increases because the orbital speed decreases.

items.q: A space probe approaches an asteroid that is irregular in shape and not of uniform density. While the probe is far away, the gravitational force on it is given accurately by F = GMm/r², with r measured from the asteroid's centre of mass. Close to the asteroid's surface the same equation is no longer accurate. Which statement explains these observations?
items.correct: Far away, the asteroid's size is negligible compared with r, so it acts as a point mass; close up, its mass is not distributed spherically, so its field is not that of a point mass at its centre.
items.misconception: The point-mass model needs the probe's mass to be negligible compared with the asteroid's; an asteroid is so small that this condition only holds while the probe is far away, and it breaks down as the probe closes in.
items.why: 'Point mass' is heard as 'tiny mass', and in examples the point masses are usually the small bodies (a satellite, an apple). The large mass ratio in these examples is then mistaken for the reason the model works. The model depends on geometry: outside a uniform sphere the field is exactly that of a point mass at the centre, whatever the sphere's mass. The Sun, the most massive body in the Solar System, is treated as a point mass in calculating planetary orbits.
items.specStatementText: conditions under which extended bodies can be treated as point masses
items.random_wrong: No body acts as a point mass when it is close: even a sphere of uniform density can be treated as a point mass at its centre only when the distance to it is large compared with its radius, as here.

items.q: Two identical stars, each of mass M, are at rest with their centres a distance r apart. A student argues that each star 'has' a gravitational potential energy of −GM²/r in the field of the other, so that the total gravitational potential energy of the two-star system is −2GM²/r. Which statement correctly assesses this claim?
items.correct: The claim double-counts: −GM²/r is the whole work done in bringing the stars together from infinite separation, and belongs to the pair, not to either star.
items.misconception: The claim is right: potential energy belongs to a body placed in a field, and each star sits in the gravitational field of the other, so each star has −GM²/r of its own.
items.why: Everyday and GCSE language ('the ball has potential energy', 'the satellite's potential energy') attaches the energy to one object; the Earth is left out of the description, so the idea that the energy resides in the system is never met. Say 'the potential energy of the Earth–satellite system'. E_p = −G m₁m₂/r is one quantity for the pair, equal to the work done to assemble it; it is not doubled by counting each body.
items.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential energy E_p of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of the components of the system
items.random_wrong: The claim has the sign wrong: work must be done against gravity to bring the stars together from infinity, so each star has +GM²/r and the total for the two is +2GM²/r.

items.q: A graph shows the gravitational potential V_g along a radial line from the centre of a planet, plotted against the distance r from the centre. Which statement about the gravitational field strength g at a point outside the planet on this line is correct?
items.correct: g is minus the gradient of the graph at that point, so the field is directed towards lower V_g.
items.misconception: g is the gradient of the graph at that point, so the field is directed towards higher V_g, outwards.
items.why: The minus sign is easily dropped when the gradient is calculated, and students picture things 'going up the potential' as the natural direction. Masses fall to lower potential energy, just as they fall downwards near the Earth. The minus sign in g = −ΔV_g/Δr expresses this: if V_g increases outwards (ΔV_g/Δr positive), g is negative, pointing inwards towards the mass.
items.specStatementText: the gravitational field strength g as the gravitational potential gradient as given by g = −ΔV_g/Δr
items.random_wrong: g is fixed by the value of V_g at that point alone, and does not depend on how V_g changes with r near the point.

items.q: The Earth has mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m, and the gravitational field strength at its surface is 9.8 N kg⁻¹. Take G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². An equipotential surface around the Earth has gravitational potential V_g = −2.50 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. What is the radius of this surface, measured from the centre of the Earth?
items.why:
Both are 'per unit mass' quantities that describe the same field, both fall with distance, and they are introduced close together with similar-looking equations (GM/r² and −GM/r). Students blur force and energy in the same way in mechanics. Keep the two chains separate: force → force per unit mass = field strength g (N kg⁻¹, vector); energy → energy per unit mass = potential V_g (J kg⁻¹, scalar). They are linked by g = −ΔV_g/Δr, so the field is the slope of the potential, not the potential itself.

Working: V_g = −GM/r, so r = GM/|V_g| = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)(5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)/(2.50 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹) = 3.982 × 10¹⁴ / 2.50 × 10⁷ = 1.593 × 10⁷ m ≈ 1.59 × 10⁷ m. This is about 2.5 Earth radii from the centre, i.e. a height of 9.56 × 10⁶ m above the surface.
items.specStatementText: equipotential surfaces for gravitational fields
items.working: V_g = −GM/r, so r = GM/|V_g| = (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²)(5.97 × 10²⁴ kg)/(2.50 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹) = 3.982 × 10¹⁴ / 2.50 × 10⁷ = 1.593 × 10⁷ m ≈ 1.59 × 10⁷ m. This is about 2.5 Earth radii from the centre, i.e. a height of 9.56 × 10⁶ m above the surface.

items.q: A small mass is at a point P on an equipotential surface in the gravitational field of a planet. It is to be moved a short distance from P. In which direction should it be moved so that the gravitational force does the greatest positive work on it?
items.correct: Perpendicular to the equipotential surface and towards the planet, so that it moves along the field line through P towards lower potential.
items.misconception: Along the equipotential surface, because the gravitational field acts along the surface rather than across it.
items.why: Both are drawn as lines on field diagrams, and 'along the field' and 'along the equipotential' sound alike. Students memorise that the two are related without the geometry. g = −ΔV_g/Δr: the field points in the direction of fastest decrease in potential, which is at right angles to the surfaces on which potential is constant. Around a planet the radial field lines cut the spherical equipotentials perpendicularly.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between equipotential surfaces and gravitational field lines
items.random_wrong: Perpendicular to the equipotential surface and away from the planet, so that it moves towards higher potential more quickly.

items.q: A satellite in a low circular orbit around a planet experiences a small viscous drag force from the thin upper atmosphere. Over many orbits it spirals slowly inwards, its orbit remaining approximately circular. Which statement about the energy changes is correct?
items.correct: The kinetic energy of the satellite increases, because the fall in potential energy exceeds the energy transferred to the atmosphere by drag.
items.misconception: The total energy of the satellite–planet system is unchanged, because the loss of gravitational potential energy equals the gain in kinetic energy.
items.why: Conservation of energy is practised almost entirely on frictionless problems, so 'energy is conserved' is applied as a rule for the satellite alone without asking where the work done by drag goes. Apply energy conservation to the whole system, including the atmosphere: E_k + E_p of the satellite falls by the energy transferred to the atmosphere. Because E_p falls by twice the total energy loss, E_k still rises, but by less than E_p falls.
items.specStatementText: the qualitative effect of a small viscous drag force due to the atmosphere on the height and speed of an orbiting body.
items.random_wrong: The kinetic energy of the satellite decreases, because the drag force acts against its motion and so does negative work on it throughout.

items.q: Is the constant in Kepler's third law, T²/r³, the same for every orbit in the universe?
items.correct: No. For circular orbits T²/r³ = 4π²/GM, where M is the mass of the central body. It is the same for all planets of the Sun, but different for the moons of Jupiter or satellites of the Earth.
items.misconception: T²/r³ is a universal constant, so the same value applies to planets round the Sun, moons round Jupiter and satellites round the Earth.
items.why: Kepler stated the law for the planets of the Sun, and it is usually taught with only that example. The word 'law' suggests a universal constant, like G. Derive the law: GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r gives T²/r³ = 4π²/GM. The constant contains the central mass M, so every central body has its own value. This is exactly how the masses of planets are found from the orbits of their moons.
items.specStatementText: Kepler’s three laws of orbital motion
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In Kepler's third law, what power of the radius is the period proportional to?
items.correct: T ∝ r^(3/2), from T² ∝ r³. Increasing r by a factor k increases T by a factor k^(3/2).
items.misconception: Kepler's third law is recalled with the wrong powers, most often as T ∝ r², by association with the inverse-square law.
items.why: The inverse-square law is the relationship most strongly associated with gravity, so 'squared' is attached to the radius. Students who memorise the law as 'T squared, r cubed' can still misplace the powers when scaling. Derive rather than recall: GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r gives T² = 4π²r³/GM, so T² ∝ r³. To scale, cube the radius ratio and then take the square root: T₂ = T₁ × (r₂/r₁)^(3/2).
items.specStatementText: Kepler’s three laws of orbital motion
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the Sun at the centre of a planet's elliptical orbit?
items.correct: No. By Kepler's first law the Sun is at one focus of the ellipse, which is off-centre. The distance from the Sun therefore varies around the orbit.
items.misconception: The Sun is at the centre of each planet's elliptical orbit.
items.why: Most diagrams show near-circular orbits centred on the Sun, and for a circle the centre and the focus coincide. The word 'focus' is unfamiliar. An ellipse has two foci on its long axis, symmetrically placed either side of the centre. The Sun sits at one of them, the other is empty. The planet is nearest the Sun at the end of the long axis next to the occupied focus, and furthest at the other end.
items.specStatementText: Kepler’s three laws of orbital motion
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a small body exert any gravitational pull on a much larger one?
items.correct: Yes. Every mass attracts every other mass. A small body pulls a large one with exactly the same force as the large body pulls it.
items.misconception: Only large bodies such as planets have gravity; a small body exerts no gravitational pull on a much larger one.
items.why: Gravity is only ever noticed for planets and stars; the attraction between everyday objects is far too small to feel. Students therefore treat gravity as a property of big bodies rather than of all mass. Newton's law applies to every pair of masses: F = Gm₁m₂/r² is non-zero whenever both masses are non-zero, and it is the same force on each. A falling apple pulls the Earth up with a force equal to its own weight; the Earth's acceleration is simply immeasurably small.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s universal law of gravitation as given by F = G m₁m₂/r² for bodies treated as point masses
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does gravity need air, so that there is no gravity where there is no atmosphere?
items.correct: No. Gravitational attraction depends only on mass and distance and acts across empty space. The Moon has no atmosphere but has a gravitational field; the Sun's gravity reaches the Earth across a vacuum.
items.misconception: Gravity depends on an atmosphere: a body with no air, such as the Moon, has no gravity, and there is no gravity in space above the atmosphere.
items.why: Pictures of astronauts floating in orbit, and phrases such as 'zero gravity' and 'weightless in space', suggest gravity stops where the air stops. Students also link gravity with air pressure pushing things down. This is widely documented in studies of children's and students' ideas about gravity. Gravity acts through a vacuum: the Moon orbits the Earth and the planets orbit the Sun across empty space. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are falling freely together, not because gravity is absent; at the height of the International Space Station g is still about 90% of its surface value.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s universal law of gravitation as given by F = G m₁m₂/r² for bodies treated as point masses
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can a distance given in kilometres be substituted directly into F = GMm/r²?
items.correct: No. G is in N m² kg⁻², so r must be in metres. A distance in km must be multiplied by 10³ before it is squared.
items.misconception: Distances quoted in km can be substituted directly into the gravitation equations without converting to metres.
items.why: Orbital heights and planetary radii are usually quoted in km, and students convert units less carefully when a number already looks 'large enough'. Because r is squared, the error is a factor of 10⁶ in F or g. Convert every distance to metres before substituting: G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² is defined with metres. 6970 km = 6.97 × 10⁶ m. An error of 10³ in r becomes 10⁶ in r², which is why unconverted answers are absurdly large.
items.specStatementText: Newton’s universal law of gravitation as given by F = G m₁m₂/r² for bodies treated as point masses
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a planet's gravity come from its centre because its mass is actually concentrated there?
items.correct: No. Every part of the planet attracts the satellite. For a uniform sphere the combined pull of all the parts is the same as if the mass were at the centre; the mass itself is spread through the whole volume.
items.misconception: Gravity comes from the centre of a planet, where its mass is really concentrated, so only the centre attracts objects.
items.why: Diagrams show forces acting at the centre of a planet, and the phrase 'as if the mass were concentrated at the centre' is remembered without the 'as if'. Some students also picture gravity as coming from the Earth's core. The mass of a uniform sphere is spread evenly through its volume, and each part attracts the satellite. The pulls from the near and far parts, and from either side, combine to give a resultant equal to that of a point mass at the centre. This is a mathematical result about the sum of the forces, not a statement about where the mass is.
items.specStatementText: conditions under which extended bodies can be treated as point masses
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is g equal to 9.8 N kg⁻¹ everywhere?
items.correct: No. 9.8 N kg⁻¹ is the value at the Earth's surface. g = GM/r², so it is different on other planets and decreases with height above the Earth.
items.misconception: The gravitational field strength (or acceleration of free fall) has the value 9.8 m s⁻² at every point, on any planet and at any height.
items.why: g = 9.8 m s⁻² is used in almost every mechanics calculation, where it is treated as a constant, and is sometimes called 'the gravitational constant', blurring it with G. g = GM/r² depends on the mass of the body producing the field and on the distance from its centre. It is about 1.6 N kg⁻¹ on the Moon's surface, 3.7 N kg⁻¹ on Mars and 0.22 N kg⁻¹ at the height of a geostationary satellite. G, not g, is the universal constant.
items.specStatementText: that gravitational field strength g at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by g = F/m = GM/r²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a smaller planet always have a weaker gravitational field at its surface?
items.correct: No. Surface g = GM/R² depends on the mass and the radius together. A planet with the same mass but a smaller radius has a stronger surface field, because its surface is closer to its centre.
items.misconception: The gravitational field strength at a planet's surface depends on how big the planet is: a smaller planet has a weaker field and a bigger one a stronger field.
items.why: In the Solar System the larger planets are usually also the more massive, so size and gravity are linked in students' minds. Films and books describe small bodies as having 'low gravity' because they are small. Use g = GM/R². Mass and radius are separate variables: at the same mass, halving the radius makes the surface field four times stronger, which is why white dwarfs and neutron stars, small but massive, have enormous surface fields.
items.specStatementText: that gravitational field strength g at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by g = F/m = GM/r²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the point of zero resultant field between two bodies their centre of mass?
items.correct: No. The centre of mass is where the masses balance, x₁M₁ = x₂M₂. The zero-field point is where the field strengths balance, M₁/x₁² = M₂/x₂². They are at very different places, on opposite sides of the midpoint.
items.misconception: The point between two bodies at which their gravitational fields cancel is their centre of mass, the balance point of the system.
items.why: Both are described as the point where the two bodies 'balance', and both lie on the line joining them. The centre of mass has just been used in orbital contexts, so it is the balance point students reach for. The centre of mass balances masses times distances and lies close to the more massive body (for the Earth–Moon system it is inside the Earth). The zero-field point balances masses divided by distances squared and lies close to the less massive body. Always write the condition g₁ = g₂ and solve it.
items.specStatementText: that gravitational field strength g at a point is the force per unit mass experienced by a small point mass at that point as given by g = F/m = GM/r²
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the Earth's gravity caused by its magnetism?
items.correct: No. Gravity is an attraction between masses; magnetism is a separate interaction between magnets and currents. Gravity acts on all matter, including non-magnetic materials, and its field lines are radial, not loops.
items.misconception: Gravity is a form of magnetism, so the Earth's gravitational field lines loop out of one pole and back into the other, like its magnetic field.
items.why: Both are described as invisible pulls from the Earth, magnets 'pull things towards them', and the Earth's magnetic field is drawn in the same lessons. This is a well-documented confusion in research on students' ideas about gravity. Gravity acts on every mass: wood, water, plastic and people all fall, though none is magnetic. The Moon, which has almost no magnetic field, still has a gravitational field. Gravitational field lines around a sphere are straight and radial, pointing inwards, and never form closed loops.
items.specStatementText: gravitational field lines.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does gravity point in one fixed direction, 'down', everywhere?
items.correct: No. Gravity points towards the centre of the attracting body. 'Down' in Australia is the opposite direction to 'down' in Europe; the field is radial, and only over a small region does it look parallel.
items.misconception: Gravity acts in a single fixed direction, 'down', everywhere, so the field lines are parallel and equally spaced at any distance from the planet.
items.why: Everyday experience is of a uniform field: things fall 'down', and diagrams of a small region near the surface show parallel lines. Research on children's ideas about the Earth's shape and gravity shows many students keep a single absolute 'down'. 'Down' is towards the planet's centre. Around a whole planet the field lines are radial, converging on the centre and spreading apart with distance. Parallel, equally spaced lines are the uniform-field approximation, valid only over a region small compared with the planet's radius.
items.specStatementText: gravitational field lines.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a gravitational field exist only along the field lines that are drawn?
items.correct: No. The field exists at every point in the region. Only a few lines are drawn, as a sample; the spacing of the lines shows the strength, and the field is present in the gaps between them.
items.misconception: The field exists only along the lines drawn, so there is no field (no force) in the gaps between the field lines.
items.why: Lines on a diagram look like physical things, such as strings or rails, and students take the drawing literally. The number of lines drawn is arbitrary, which they are rarely told. Field lines are a representation. A mass placed between two drawn lines experiences a force just as one placed on a line does; its direction is between that of the neighbouring lines. More lines could be drawn anywhere without changing the field.
items.specStatementText: gravitational field lines.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must positive work be done to bring two attracting masses together from infinity?
items.correct: No. The masses attract, so the gravitational force does positive work as they approach. To bring them together without them gaining kinetic energy, an external agent must hold them back and does negative work. This is why E_p is negative.
items.misconception: Positive work must be done to bring two masses together from infinite separation, and the minus sign in E_p is just a convention.
items.why: Students think of 'assembling' as effort and link any work done by an agent with putting energy in. The idea that an agent does negative work by holding something back is unfamiliar. Picture the masses approaching from infinity: gravity pulls them together and would speed them up. To assemble the system slowly, the agent pulls against the motion, so the agent's force is opposite to the displacement and its work is negative. E_p, the work done to assemble the system, is therefore negative. The sign follows from the definition and zero at infinity; it is not an arbitrary convention.
items.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential energy E_p of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of the components of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a negative potential energy mean that energy has been used up?
items.correct: No. A negative E_p means the system has less energy than it would at infinite separation. No energy has been destroyed: as the bodies came together, E_p was transferred to other stores such as kinetic energy.
items.misconception: A negative potential energy means energy has been used up, so the system is left with an energy 'deficit'.
items.why: Everyday language speaks of energy being 'used up', and a negative number looks like a debt. Students with the used-up view of energy read the sign as evidence that energy has been consumed. Energy is conserved. When two attracting bodies move together, the decrease in E_p equals the increase in other stores (kinetic energy, or internal energy if they collide). The negative value only reflects the choice of zero at infinity: the bound system has less energy than the separated one.
items.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential energy E_p of a system is the work done to assemble the system from infinite separation of the components of the system
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a mass is lifted a large distance, can the field strength at the final height be used for the whole journey?
items.correct: No. The field changes continuously along the path, so no single end-point value of g gives the work done. The exact change is found from E_p = −GMm/r.
items.misconception: The work done lifting a mass through a large height can be found with the field strength at the final position, as though that value applied over the whole path.
items.why: Students who know that g falls with height try to 'correct' mgΔh by using the new, smaller g, without realising that g varies throughout the journey. Near the surface the field is strong, and most of the work is done there. Using the final (weakest) value of g ignores this and underestimates the work. The potential energy equation accounts for the variation exactly: ΔE_p = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
items.specStatementText: the gravitational potential energy for a two-body system as given by E_p = −G m₁m₂/r where r is the separation between the centre of mass of the two bodies
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: When a mass is lifted a large distance, does the mean of the starting and final field strengths give the work done?
items.correct: No. The mean of the end values of g works only for a quantity that varies linearly with distance. g varies as 1/r², so its arithmetic mean over the path is not (g₁ + g₂)/2; the exact change is found from E_p = −GMm/r.
items.misconception: Because g changes with height, the work done can be found using the mean of the starting and final field strengths, (g₁ + g₂)/2, as if g fell linearly.
items.why: In kinematics s = ((u + v)/2)t is used for uniform acceleration, where velocity does change linearly, and students carry the 'average of the ends' habit to quantities that do not vary linearly. An average of end values is exact only for a linear variation. For g ∝ 1/r² the curve bends, so (g₁ + g₂)/2 overestimates the mean field. The work done is the area under the force–distance graph, which the potential energy equation gives exactly: ΔE_p = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂).
items.specStatementText: the gravitational potential energy for a two-body system as given by E_p = −G m₁m₂/r where r is the separation between the centre of mass of the two bodies

items.q: Is gravitational potential zero at the planet's surface and positive above it?
items.correct: No. In the IB course the zero of gravitational potential is at infinity. At the surface V_g = −GM/R, and V_g is negative at every finite distance, rising towards zero with height.
items.misconception: Gravitational potential (and potential energy) is zero at the surface of a planet and positive above it, as with mgh.
items.why: Before this topic, E_p = mgh was always measured from the ground, with E_p = 0 at the surface. That reference point is carried over to V_g. V_g = −GM/r takes infinity as zero, because only at infinity is the effect of the planet absent for every planet alike. With this choice V_g is negative everywhere; moving away from the planet it increases towards zero. Changes in V_g are the same whichever zero is chosen, but values are not.
items.specStatementText: that the gravitational potential V_g at a point is the work done per unit mass in bringing a mass from infinity to that point as given by V_g = −GM/r
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the kinetic energy of a satellite in orbit equal to GMm/r?
items.correct: No. GMm/r² = mv²/r gives mv² = GMm/r, so E_k = ½mv² = GMm/2r. Forgetting the ½ doubles the kinetic energy.
items.misconception: The kinetic energy of an orbiting satellite is GMm/r, taken directly from mv² = GMm/r without the ½.
items.why: The derivation gives mv² = GMm/r, and in a multi-step calculation the ½ in E_k = ½mv² is easily dropped. Always finish the step: E_k = ½mv² = ½(GMm/r) = GMm/2r. A useful check is that in a circular orbit E_k = −½E_p and the total energy is −GMm/2r.
items.specStatementText: the work done in moving a mass m in a gravitational field as given by W = mΔV_g
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the energy needed to put a satellite into orbit just its kinetic energy in orbit?
items.correct: No. The satellite also gains gravitational potential energy in rising from the surface to the orbit. The energy needed is ΔE_p + E_k.
items.misconception: Getting into orbit only means reaching orbital speed, so the energy needed is the satellite's kinetic energy in orbit; gaining height needs no extra energy.
items.why: Launches are described in terms of the speed needed ('about 8 km s⁻¹ to reach orbit'), and students treat the orbit as a matter of speed alone, forgetting the work done against gravity to climb. Energy conservation from rest on the surface to the orbit: energy supplied = (E_p,orbit − E_p,surface) + E_k,orbit = GMm(1/R − 1/r) + GMm/2r. Both terms are needed.
items.specStatementText: the work done in moving a mass m in a gravitational field as given by W = mΔV_g

items.q: Are equipotential surfaces the same as field lines?
items.correct: No. Field lines show the direction of the force; equipotentials join points of equal potential. They cross at right angles: around a planet the field lines are radial and the equipotentials are concentric spheres.
items.misconception: Equipotentials are another name for field lines, so around a planet they are radial lines pointing towards the centre.
items.why: Both are sets of lines drawn on the same field diagrams, and both are said to 'map' the field. Students blur the two representations. The two are perpendicular. Moving along a field line changes the potential most rapidly; moving along an equipotential does not change it at all. Around a sphere: radial field lines, spherical equipotentials.
items.specStatementText: equipotential surfaces for gravitational fields
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a force always do work on an object moving while it acts?
items.correct: No. A force does work only if it has a component along the displacement: W = Fs cos θ. A force perpendicular to the motion does no work.
items.misconception: Whenever a force acts on a moving object it does work on it, whatever the angle between the force and the motion.
items.why: Everyday 'work' is effort, and effort seems to be needed whenever a force acts on something moving. The cos θ in W = Fs cos θ is often treated as optional. Work is done only by the component of force along the displacement. Along an equipotential the gravitational force is perpendicular to the motion (cos 90° = 0), so it does no work and the kinetic energy of a satellite in a circular orbit stays constant.
items.specStatementText: the relationship between equipotential surfaces and gravitational field lines

items.q: Is the escape speed twice the orbital speed?
items.correct: No. At the same r, v_esc = √(2GM/r) and v_orbital = √(GM/r), so v_esc = √2 × v_orbital ≈ 1.41 v_orbital. The kinetic energy needed to escape is twice the orbital kinetic energy.
items.misconception: The escape speed at a point is twice the orbital speed there, so escaping needs four times the orbital kinetic energy.
items.why: The two equations differ by a factor of 2, and students attach the 2 to the speed rather than to the quantity under the square root. Compare kinetic energies rather than speeds: escape needs ½mv² = GMm/r, orbit has ½mv² = GMm/2r. The kinetic energy doubles, so the speed rises by √2, not 2.
items.specStatementText: the escape speed v_esc at any point in a gravitational field as given by v_esc = √(2GM/r)

items.q: Is escape impossible because the gravitational field never becomes zero?
items.correct: No. The field extends to infinity but weakens as 1/r², so the total work needed to reach infinity, GMm/r, is finite. 'Escape' means having enough energy never to fall back, not reaching a place without gravity.
items.misconception: A body can never escape a planet's gravity, because the field never falls to zero, so an infinite amount of energy would be needed.
items.why: Students are told that gravitational fields have infinite range and conclude that the pull can never be overcome. 'Escape' is pictured as reaching a place beyond gravity's reach. The work needed to move a mass to infinity is the area under the force–distance graph, which for F ∝ 1/r² is finite: GMm/r. A body with at least this kinetic energy slows down forever but never stops or turns back; that is what escape means.
items.specStatementText: the escape speed v_esc at any point in a gravitational field as given by v_esc = √(2GM/r)

items.q: If a satellite moves more slowly in its new orbit, does it have less total energy?
items.correct: No. A slower (higher) orbit has less kinetic energy but more potential energy, and the gain in E_p is twice the loss in E_k, so the total energy is higher.
items.misconception: A slower satellite has less total energy, so moving to a higher, slower orbit lowers the satellite's total energy.
items.why: Students equate a body's energy with its kinetic energy and forget that potential energy changes too, and in this case changes by more. Add both stores: E = E_k + E_p = GMm/2r − GMm/r = −GMm/2r. As r increases this becomes less negative, so the total energy increases even though the speed falls.
items.specStatementText: the orbital speed v_orbital of a body orbiting a large mass as given by v_orbital = √(GM/r)

items.q: Because drag lowers a satellite's speed, and higher orbits are slower, does drag raise the orbit?
items.correct: No. Drag removes energy, and a satellite with less total energy (−GMm/2r more negative) is in a smaller orbit. The satellite spirals inwards and its speed increases.
items.misconception: Drag reduces the satellite's speed, and since v = √(GM/r) means slower orbits are larger, the satellite moves out to a larger orbit.
items.why: Students correctly link slower speed with larger orbits in v = √(GM/r), and correctly expect drag to oppose motion, then combine the two without considering energy. Start from energy, not speed. Drag does negative work, so the total energy −GMm/2r decreases, which means r decreases. With a smaller r, v = √(GM/r) is larger. The satellite loses height and gains speed.
items.specStatementText: the qualitative effect of a small viscous drag force due to the atmosphere on the height and speed of an orbiting body.
